questions.stem: In a histologic study of an implantation site about 2 weeks after fertilization, a population of fetal-derived cells is found that secretes enzymes easing the burrowing of the overlying cell layer into the endometrium, continually supplies new cells that relocate into that overlying layer, and forms columns that invade maternal arteries. Which of the following cell populations is being described?

explanation.summary: The cytotrophoblast (inner trophoblast layer) makes invasion enzymes, feeds new cells to the syncytiotrophoblast, and forms columns that invade maternal arteries.
explanation.whyCorrect: The trophoblast has an outer syncytiotrophoblast and an inner cytotrophoblast. The cytotrophoblast produces enzymes that help the syncytiotrophoblast burrow into the endometrium, is a source of new cells that relocate to the syncytiotrophoblast, and forms columns that invade maternal arteries to establish the uteroplacental circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Decidual cells are maternal, progesterone-modified endometrium, not fetal cells that invade maternal arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These maternal NK cells regulate invasion depth and spiral artery remodeling but are not fetal-derived and do not become syncytium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myometrium is the maternal tissue invaded (inner third); it does not supply trophoblast cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer layer that does the burrowing and receives new cells; it is not the source of the enzymes and relocating cells.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation has a blood pressure of 166/110 mm Hg, 3+ proteinuria, elevated serum transaminases, and a rising serum creatinine. Her blood pressure was normal before 20 weeks. A defect in which of the following early pregnancy processes most likely underlies her condition?

choices.label: B
choices.text: hCG rescue of the corpus luteum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trophoblast invasion of the uterine wall

explanation.summary: Preeclampsia is caused by faulty trophoblast implantation into the uterine wall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Preeclampsia (hypertension with endothelial dysfunction, usually after 20 weeks) results from faulty implantation of the trophoblast in the uterine wall. The improper implantation disrupts placental blood flow and triggers systemic inflammation, producing maternal organ dysfunction such as liver and kidney damage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fas ligand protects the fetus by inducing maternal T-cell apoptosis; it is not the lesion in preeclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Failed luteal rescue would cause loss of progesterone support early in pregnancy, not preeclampsia after 20 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: hPL alters maternal glucose and lipid metabolism; it is not the cause of preeclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure to shed the zona pellucida would prevent implantation altogether rather than cause late-onset hypertension.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has a positive pregnancy test 4 weeks after her last menstrual period. In a nonconception cycle, the declining luteal stimulation late in the cycle would allow her corpus luteum to shrink and sex hormone levels to fall. Which of the following hormones prevents this and keeps the corpus luteum secreting progesterone?

explanation.summary: hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast rescues the corpus luteum so it keeps making progesterone, estrogen, and relaxin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Late in the cycle LH is insufficient to maintain the corpus luteum. After implantation, hCG secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast stimulates the corpus luteum to keep producing progesterone, estrogen, and relaxin during the first 10 weeks of pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Placental CRH stimulates prostaglandins and DHEA to help induce contractions at term.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen is secreted by the corpus luteum under hCG stimulation; it is not the rescuing signal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: hPL alters maternal metabolism to supply the fetus; it does not act on luteal cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin is itself a product of the corpus luteum early in pregnancy; it does not sustain the corpus luteum.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 15 weeks' gestation undergoes removal of the ovary containing the corpus luteum because of torsion. She receives no hormone supplementation, and the pregnancy continues without complication. Which of the following best explains the maintenance of her progesterone levels?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placental lactogen now substitutes for it

explanation.summary: After about 10 weeks the syncytiotrophoblast makes progesterone and estrogen, so the corpus luteum is no longer needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: hCG-driven corpus luteum production of progesterone is temporary. After 10 weeks, progesterone and estrogen are produced by placental syncytiotrophoblast cells (and relaxin by cytotrophoblasts), so loss of the corpus luteum at 15 weeks does not end the pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: After week 10 cytotrophoblasts produce relaxin; progesterone and estrogen come from the syncytiotrophoblast.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The decidua is endometrium modified by progesterone; it is not the placental source of progesterone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: hPL alters maternal metabolism and does not replace progesterone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Relaxin only assists progesterone in placental growth; it does not replace progesterone.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation has a mildly elevated postprandial glucose level. A hormone synthesized by the syncytiotrophoblast is contributing by raising maternal glucose, lowering maternal glucose utilization, and increasing lipolysis so that the fetus is assured adequate nutrition. Which of the following hormones is responsible?

explanation.summary: Human placental lactogen raises maternal glucose, reduces maternal glucose use, and increases lipolysis to secure fetal nutrition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Human placental lactogen is made by the syncytiotrophoblast. It ensures adequate fetal nutrition by altering maternal metabolism: increasing glucose levels, lowering glucose utilization, and increasing lipolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CRH stimulates prostaglandins and DHEA to promote contractions at term.
whyWrongByChoice.B: hCG maintains the corpus luteum through the LH receptor; its described role is not metabolic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progesterone is the principal driver of placental growth; it is not described as shifting maternal fuel use.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin assists progesterone in placental growth and is made by cytotrophoblasts after week 10.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation asks how the sugar from her meals reaches her baby. The fetus relies on this sugar as its primary energy source. By which mechanism does it cross the placenta?

explanation.summary: Glucose, the main fetal energy source, crosses the placenta by facilitated diffusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucose moves by facilitated diffusion: passive movement down a concentration gradient via a pore or channel. It is the primary energy source for the fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Active transport is used for amino acids, water-soluble vitamins, calcium, iron, iodine, and phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fc receptor transport is the special route for maternal IgG after endocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptor-mediated endocytosis moves fatty acids, LDL cholesterol, and IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Simple/passive diffusion is used for gases, water, sodium, fat-soluble vitamins, and waste products.

questions.stem: A medical student reviewing placental transport notes that some nutrients require energy expenditure to cross the membrane. Which of the following crosses the placenta by active transport?

explanation.summary: Amino acids cross the placenta by active transport.
explanation.whyCorrect: Active transport, movement across a membrane that requires energy, is used for amino acids as well as water-soluble vitamins, calcium, iron, iodine, and phosphate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fatty acids cross by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose crosses by facilitated diffusion, a passive process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxygen crosses by passive diffusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sodium crosses by passive diffusion.

questions.stem: In the placenta, carbon dioxide diffuses from fetal red blood cells into the maternal circulation, where it is later removed by the maternal lungs. Which of the following best describes how this carbon dioxide movement promotes oxygen uptake by the fetus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal blood acidifies, raising fetal hemoglobin O2 affinity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal blood alkalinizes, lowering fetal hemoglobin O2 affinity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fetal blood alkalinizes, raising fetal hemoglobin O2 affinity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal blood acidifies, raising maternal hemoglobin O2 affinity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Maternal blood alkalinizes, raising maternal hemoglobin O2 affinity

explanation.summary: CO2 leaving fetal blood makes it alkaline, raising fetal hemoglobin's O2 affinity (double Bohr effect).
explanation.whyCorrect: As CO2 diffuses from fetus to mother, maternal blood becomes more acidic and fetal blood more alkaline. The alkaline pH increases the affinity of fetal hemoglobin for oxygen, while the acidic maternal pH lowers maternal hemoglobin affinity (Bohr effect), both promoting fetal O2 uptake.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fetal blood loses CO2 and becomes more alkaline, not acidic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An alkaline pH increases hemoglobin O2 affinity (Bohr effect).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acidification lowers, not raises, maternal hemoglobin O2 affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Maternal blood gains CO2 and becomes more acidic; higher maternal affinity would hinder O2 release.

questions.stem: Trophoblast cells in contact with maternal blood express an atypical cell-surface human lymphocyte antigen rather than the usual antigens. Its interaction with maternal natural killer cells and cytotoxic T cells makes them more tolerant of the fetus. Which molecule is expressed?

explanation.summary: Trophoblast HLA-G makes maternal NK cells and cytotoxic T cells tolerant of the fetus.
explanation.whyCorrect: HLAs are usually HLA-A or HLA-B antigens. The trophoblast expresses atypical HLA-G, which interacts with maternal NK cells and cytotoxic T cells when in contact with maternal blood, making them more tolerant of the fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Fas receptor is on maternal lymphocytes; the trophoblast expresses Fas ligand.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intracellular Fc receptors in the syncytiotrophoblast transport maternal IgG; they are not HLA molecules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-A is one of the usual antigens used to distinguish self from non-self, not the atypical trophoblast antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-B is one of the usual antigens; the trophoblast instead expresses atypical HLA-G.

questions.stem: In an experimental model, a drug blocks a placental enzyme that is present from about day 6 after fertilization and normally deprives maternal T cells of a nutrient they need for survival. Local concentration of which of the following substances would most likely increase?

explanation.summary: Placental IDO degrades tryptophan to kynurenine; blocking it raises tryptophan and supports maternal T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase breaks down tryptophan into kynurenine and is present from day 6. Maternal T cells need tryptophan to survive, so IDO protects the fetus by depleting it; kynurenine also inhibits T-cell development. Inhibiting IDO would increase local tryptophan.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DHEA is raised by placental CRH near term, not by this enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fas ligand is a trophoblast surface protein unrelated to this enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kynurenine is the product of IDO; blocking the enzyme lowers, not raises, kynurenine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Relaxin is a hormone from the corpus luteum and later cytotrophoblasts, not an IDO substrate.

questions.stem: Maternal T lymphocytes that come into direct contact with trophoblast cells undergo programmed cell death after a receptor-ligand interaction, reducing the chance that they target the fetus. Which of the following interactions is responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Maternal Fas ligand with trophoblast Fas receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal IgG with syncytiotrophoblast Fc receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trophoblast Fas ligand with maternal Fas receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trophoblast HLA-A with maternal cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trophoblast HLA-G with maternal NK cell receptors

explanation.summary: Trophoblast Fas ligand binds Fas receptor on maternal lymphocytes, triggering their apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trophoblast cells express Fas ligand, which interacts with the Fas receptor on maternal lymphocytes. After this interaction, maternal T lymphocytes undergo apoptosis, lowering the likelihood of an attack on the fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The direction is reversed; the ligand is on the trophoblast and the receptor on maternal lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fc receptors transport maternal IgG to the fetus; this does not kill maternal lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-A is a usual self/non-self antigen; the trophoblast expresses atypical HLA-G instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-G makes maternal NK and T cells tolerant; it is not described as inducing apoptosis.

questions.stem: Cord blood from a healthy term newborn contains high levels of maternal-derived antibody that will protect the infant for several months. These are large molecules that cannot pass freely through the placental barrier. How did they reach the fetal circulation?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leakage through breaks in chorionic villi

explanation.summary: Maternal IgG is endocytosed by the syncytiotrophoblast and carried to the fetal side on intracellular Fc receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Large IgG molecules cross via the syncytiotrophoblast by a unique mechanism: they are first taken up by endocytosis and then bind intracellular Fc receptors that transport them to the fetal side. This occurs during the last trimester and gives passive immunity lasting several months.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Active transport is used for amino acids and some minerals and vitamins, not IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Facilitated diffusion via channels is the route for glucose, not IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The placenta maintains a barrier between maternal and fetal cells; IgG uses a specific mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Large IgG molecules do not diffuse passively; they are taken up by the syncytiotrophoblast.

questions.stem: About 4 days after fertilization, the single-celled zygote has become a solid 16-cell structure that will evolve into the implanting form on days 5-6. What is this 16-cell structure called?

explanation.summary: The zygote becomes a 16-cell morula by about day 4, then a blastocyst on days 5-6.
explanation.whyCorrect: After fertilization the zygote transforms into a 16-cell morula about day 4. During days 5-6, the morula evolves into the blastocyst, which implants in the endometrium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The blastocyst forms from the morula on days 5-6 and is what implants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The decidua is the progesterone-modified maternal endometrium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The trophoblast is the outer cell layer of the blastocyst, evident around day 6.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The zygote is the single-celled product of the merged gamete nuclei.

questions.stem: At delivery, a layer of maternal tissue derived from endometrium that was thickened under high progesterone levels is shed with the placenta as afterbirth. Which tissue is this?

explanation.summary: The decidua is progesterone-modified endometrium forming the maternal side of the placenta, shed as afterbirth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under high maternal progesterone, the endometrium thickens and becomes the decidua: enlarged cells surrounded by rich vasculature and connective tissue. It is the maternal side of the placenta and is shed as afterbirth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chorionic villi are fetal projections formed from both trophoblast layers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The cytotrophoblast is the inner fetal trophoblast layer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myometrium is uterine smooth muscle; only its inner third is invaded and it is not shed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The syncytiotrophoblast is fetal trophoblast, not modified maternal endometrium.

questions.stem: A blastocyst arrives in the uterine cavity but is unable to make even an initial loose connection between its outer cell layer and the decidua. Which event must occur before this first attachment step can take place?

explanation.summary: The blastocyst first sheds its zona pellucida, then proceeds through apposition, adhesion, and invasion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first step of implantation is shedding of the outer glycoprotein coat, the zona pellucida. Only then can apposition, a loose connection between the trophoblast and decidua, occur, followed by adhesion and invasion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chorionic villi form after invasion, around 2 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor-ligand binding forms the stronger connection of the adhesion step, after apposition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enzyme secretion belongs to the later invasion step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myometrial invasion occurs well after the initial attachment.

questions.stem: During implantation, the trophoblast converts a loose contact with the uterine lining into a stronger attachment using newly made cytoskeleton and receptor-ligand interactions, including proteoglycan receptors. Which step of implantation is this?

explanation.summary: Adhesion is the step in which the trophoblast attaches firmly via new cytoskeleton and receptor-ligand interactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: In adhesion, a stronger connection is established: the trophoblast penetrates the endometrium and attaches using newly made cytoskeleton and receptor-ligand interactions, including proteoglycan receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Apposition is the earlier loose connection between trophoblast and decidua.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The morula forms around day 4, before implantation begins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Invasion is the deeper penetration into stroma and vessels driven by secreted enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shedding of the glycoprotein coat precedes any contact with the decidua.

questions.stem: A blastocyst sheds its glycoprotein coat and attaches firmly to the endometrium but is unable to secrete the enzymes that break down the decidua. Which step of implantation will fail?

explanation.summary: Invasion requires blastocyst enzymes that break down the decidua to penetrate stroma and uterine vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The invasion step involves deeper penetration into the stroma and uterine blood vessels, and the blastocyst secretes enzymes that break down the decidua for it. Without those enzymes, invasion fails even if apposition and adhesion succeed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stem states firm attachment occurred, which is adhesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Apposition, the loose initial connection, has already occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.D: That transition occurs on days 5-6, before implantation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The stem states the glycoprotein coat was shed.

questions.stem: In a normal pregnancy, the syncytiotrophoblast progressively penetrates the decidua and the uterine vasculature. What is the normal deepest extent of its invasion into the uterine wall?

explanation.summary: Syncytiotrophoblast normally invades the entire endometrium and the inner third of the myometrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The syncytiotrophoblast progressively penetrates the decidua, invading the entire endometrium, the inner third of the myometrium, and the uterine vasculature. Maternal NK cells help ensure the penetration reaches the correct depth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Normal invasion extends past the endometrium into the inner myometrium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Normal invasion stops at the inner third of the myometrium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Invasion normally reaches only the inner third of the myometrium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The syncytiotrophoblast invades the entire endometrium, not just its surface.

questions.stem: The chorionic villi are finger-like projections formed by the two trophoblast layers. Nutrient and gas exchange occurs across them because the spaces between the villi fill with which of the following?

explanation.summary: The spaces between chorionic villi fill with maternal blood for mother-fetus exchange.
explanation.whyCorrect: Together the cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast form chorionic villi with spaces between them. These spaces fill with maternal blood and allow nutrient and gas exchange between mother and baby.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amniotic fluid surrounds the fetus, not the villi.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The decidua is the maternal tissue invaded, not what fills the intervillous spaces.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fetal blood lies within the villi and reaches the fetus through the umbilical cord.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The intervillous spaces fill with maternal blood, not lymph.

questions.stem: Maternal immune cells present in large numbers at the implantation site aid implantation and placental maturation and ensure that placental tissue penetrates the uterine wall to the correct depth. Which type of cell are these?

explanation.summary: Maternal large granular lymphocytes (NK cells) aid implantation and set the depth of placental invasion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal large granular lymphocytes are natural killer cells present in large numbers at the implantation site. They aid implantation and placental maturation and ensure placental tissue penetrates the uterine wall at the correct depth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T cells are made tolerant by HLA-G; they are not the cells regulating invasion depth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytotrophoblasts are fetal, not maternal immune cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decidual cells are modified endometrial cells, not immune cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells are not described as regulating placental invasion.

questions.stem: At the uteroplacental interface, maternal immune cells disrupt extracellular matrix components around the spiral arteries without destroying the surrounding tissue. What is the intended vascular result of this remodeling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Destruction of the surrounding decidual tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dilated capacitance vessels for greater flow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Narrowed vessels that limit placental flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: New umbilical arteries from fetal iliac vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombosed vessels that seal the implant site

explanation.summary: NK-cell remodeling of spiral arteries creates dilated capacitance vessels to handle increased gestational blood flow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal granular lymphocytes balance spiral artery remodeling (by disrupting extracellular matrix) against destruction of surrounding tissue. The remodeling creates dilated capacitance vessels in the uteroplacental vasculature to accommodate the increased blood flow of gestation; poor regulation leads to preeclampsia, stillbirth, and fetal growth restriction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tissue destruction is the unwanted side of the tightrope that must be avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Remodeling widens vessels to accommodate the increased flow of gestation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Umbilical arteries are fetal vessels, not products of spiral artery remodeling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Remodeling produces dilated vessels, not thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 31 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with preeclampsia. Impaired trophoblast invasion has caused uteroplacental insufficiency. Which of the following ultrasound findings is most likely?

explanation.summary: Impaired trophoblast invasion in preeclampsia can cause uteroplacental insufficiency with fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios.
explanation.whyCorrect: In preeclampsia, impaired trophoblast invasion may lead to uteroplacental insufficiency, resulting in fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Uteroplacental insufficiency is associated with decreased, not increased, amniotic fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduced placental supply causes growth restriction, not macrosomia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Uteroplacental insufficiency limits fetal supply, so fetal overgrowth is not expected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neither normal growth nor excess fluid fits uteroplacental insufficiency.

questions.stem: Over the first 20 weeks of pregnancy, uterine tissue weight increases from about 50 g to 1000 g, reflecting placental development and myometrial thickening. Which hormone is principally responsible for placental growth?

explanation.summary: Placental growth is driven principally by progesterone, assisted by estrogen and relaxin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Placental growth is principally caused by progesterone, assisted by estrogen and relaxin. These hormones increase uterine weight from about 50 g to 1000 g during the first 20 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CRH promotes prostaglandin and DHEA production for contractions at term.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen assists placental growth but is not the principal driver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: hPL alters maternal metabolism to supply the fetus rather than driving placental growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin assists placental growth but is not the principal driver.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is at 18 weeks' gestation, well past the point at which the corpus luteum is needed. Which cells are now the source of her relaxin?

explanation.summary: After week 10, relaxin comes from cytotrophoblasts, while progesterone and estrogen come from the syncytiotrophoblast.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the first 10 weeks, hCG stimulates the corpus luteum to make progesterone, estrogen, and relaxin. After 10 weeks, progesterone and estrogen are produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, and relaxin is produced by cytotrophoblasts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The corpus luteum makes relaxin only during roughly the first 10 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The decidua is modified endometrium and is not described as a relaxin source.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These maternal NK cells regulate invasion and spiral artery remodeling, not relaxin secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: After week 10 the syncytiotrophoblast makes progesterone and estrogen, not relaxin.

questions.stem: Early in pregnancy, a placental hormone rescues the corpus luteum by binding a receptor on luteal cells with greater affinity and potency than the receptor's native ligand. Which receptor does it bind?

explanation.summary: hCG binds the luteal LH receptor with greater affinity and potency than LH, sustaining the corpus luteum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Luteal cells are maintained by LH, but late-cycle LH is insufficient. After implantation, hCG binds the luteal LH receptor with greater affinity and potency than LH, causing the corpus luteum to keep secreting progesterone, estrogen, and relaxin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: hCG acts on the corpus luteum, not on a decidual receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen is a luteal product, and hCG does not act through its receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: hCG acts through the luteal LH receptor, not an FSH receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progesterone is the product being sustained, not the receptor hCG uses.

questions.stem: A urine pregnancy test detects the hormone that the placenta secretes early in pregnancy to build and maintain the placenta. Which placental cell layer secretes this hormone?

explanation.summary: hCG is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast early in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: hCG is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast early in pregnancy and is key to building and maintaining the placenta by stimulating the corpus luteum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The corpus luteum is the target of hCG, not a placental layer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The cytotrophoblast is the relaxin source after week 10 and a supplier of new syncytial cells, not the hCG source.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The decidua is maternal endometrium and does not secrete hCG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These maternal NK cells regulate invasion; hCG is attributed to the syncytiotrophoblast.

questions.stem: A placental hormone synthesized by the syncytiotrophoblast stimulates prostaglandin production and raises levels of dehydroepiandrosterone, and both actions help induce uterine contractions at term. Which hormone is this?

explanation.summary: Placental CRH stimulates prostaglandins and raises DHEA, helping induce contractions at term.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticotropin-releasing hormone is synthesized by the syncytiotrophoblast. It stimulates prostaglandin production and raises DHEA levels, both of which help induce uterine contractions at term; prostaglandins also regulate placental blood flow.

whyWrongByChoice.B: hCG sustains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: hPL alters maternal glucose and lipid metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progesterone principally drives placental growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin assists placental growth and is not described as stimulating prostaglandins.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances reaches the fetus by receptor-mediated endocytosis across the placenta?

explanation.summary: Fatty acids, LDL cholesterol, and IgG cross the placenta by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fatty acids, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and immunoglobulin G are moved across the placenta by receptor-mediated endocytosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amino acids and calcium cross by active transport.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose crosses by facilitated diffusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sodium and water cross by passive diffusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Water-soluble vitamins and iron cross by active transport.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman takes a daily prenatal vitamin and mineral supplement. Which of the following components crosses the placenta by passive diffusion?

explanation.summary: Fat-soluble vitamins (with electrolytes, sodium, water, and gases) cross by passive diffusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fat-soluble vitamins and electrolytes, sodium, water, oxygen, and carbon dioxide cross the placenta by passive diffusion, whereas water-soluble vitamins, calcium, iron, iodine, and phosphate require active transport.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium crosses by active transport.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iodine crosses by active transport.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphate crosses by active transport.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Water-soluble vitamins cross by active transport.

questions.stem: Because the fetus lacks functioning kidneys and liver, its metabolic wastes such as urea, uric acid, and creatinine must be removed. How are most of these waste products handled?

explanation.summary: Fetal wastes such as urea, uric acid, and creatinine cross by simple diffusion for maternal excretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most fetal waste products, including urea, uric acid, and creatinine, cross the placenta via simple diffusion and are excreted by the pregnant person's liver or kidneys.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Waste products cross mainly by simple diffusion, not active transport.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor-mediated endocytosis is used for fatty acids, LDL cholesterol, and IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Facilitated diffusion is the glucose route.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wastes are excreted by the mother, not stored.

questions.stem: A student traces blood leaving the fetus to return to the placenta through the umbilical cord. Which vessels carry this blood, and from where do they arise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One umbilical artery, from fetal internal iliacs

choices.label: B
choices.text: One umbilical vein, from the fetal IVC

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two umbilical arteries, from fetal internal iliacs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two umbilical veins, from the fetal IVC

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two uterine arteries, from the fetal aorta

explanation.summary: Two umbilical arteries return fetal blood from the internal iliac arteries; one umbilical vein carries blood to the fetal IVC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The uterine artery and vein supply the maternal side of the placenta. A single umbilical vein carries blood to the fetal inferior vena cava, and two umbilical arteries return blood from the fetal internal iliac arteries to the placenta.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There are two umbilical arteries, not one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The umbilical vein carries blood to the fetal IVC, not away from it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is a single umbilical vein, and it carries blood toward the fetus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uterine vessels supply the maternal side of the placenta.

questions.stem: In the placenta, a change in fetal blood directly reduces its capacity to hold carbon dioxide, so that carbon dioxide diffuses out of fetal red blood cells toward the maternal circulation. Which change is responsible?

explanation.summary: As fetal blood becomes oxygenated it holds less CO2 (Haldane effect), so CO2 moves to the mother.
explanation.whyCorrect: The double Haldane effect: as fetal blood becomes oxygenated, it has decreased ability to hold onto carbon dioxide, so CO2 diffuses from fetal red cells into maternal blood and is removed by the maternal lungs. Reciprocally, O2 release from maternal cells favors maternal CO2 loading.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fetal blood actually becomes more alkaline as CO2 leaves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deoxygenated blood holds more, not less, CO2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: O2 release from maternal cells favors maternal CO2 loading, not reduced fetal CO2 capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The fetal CO2 content falls as it is unloaded; it does not drive reduced capacity.

questions.stem: Apart from the pH differences created by carbon dioxide transfer, which additional factor promotes oxygen uptake by fetal blood in the placenta?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active transport of O2 by trophoblast

choices.label: D
choices.text: Higher O2 affinity of fetal hemoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lower O2 affinity of fetal hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Fetal hemoglobin binds oxygen with higher affinity than adult hemoglobin, favoring fetal O2 uptake.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxygen crosses the placenta by passive diffusion. In addition to the double Bohr effect, fetal hemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin; both factors promote oxygen uptake by fetal blood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxygen crosses by passive diffusion, not active transport.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The placenta maintains a barrier; maternal red cells are not taken up.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Facilitated diffusion is the glucose route; oxygen diffuses passively.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fetal hemoglobin has a higher, not lower, oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old Rh(D)-negative woman delivers an Rh(D)-positive infant and receives RhoGAM. By which mechanism does this treatment protect her future Rh-positive pregnancies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds fetal red cells before sensitization

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks anti-D IgG from crossing the placenta

choices.label: C
choices.text: It induces HLA-G expression on fetal red cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It neutralizes anti-D antibodies already formed

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stimulates fetal production of anti-D antibody

explanation.summary: RhoGAM binds fetal Rh-positive red cells in maternal blood before the maternal immune system recognizes them.
explanation.whyCorrect: In red cell isoimmunization, maternal anti-D antibodies cross the placenta and cause fetal hemolytic disease (anemia, hydrops fetalis, fetal demise). RhoGAM given to Rh-negative mothers binds fetal Rh-positive red cells in maternal circulation before the maternal immune system can recognize them, preventing sensitization that would affect future pregnancies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: RhoGAM does not block placental transfer; it prevents anti-D formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-G is a trophoblast molecule, not something RhoGAM induces.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RhoGAM prevents sensitization; it does not reverse existing anti-D.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RhoGAM acts on fetal cells in maternal circulation, not on fetal antibody production.

questions.stem: A newborn is diagnosed with a congenital infection even though the mother mounted a vigorous antibody response to the pathogen during pregnancy. Which of the following best explains why her antibody response did not fully protect the fetus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies cross only in the first trimester

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fc receptors carry IgM but not IgG

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgG antibodies cannot cross the placenta

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgM antibodies cannot cross the placenta

explanation.summary: Only IgG crosses the placenta; important antibodies such as IgM do not reach the fetus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital infections remain possible because only IgG antibodies can cross the placenta. Important antibodies such as IgM are not present to protect the fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Maternal IgG crosses mainly during the last trimester.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fc receptors transport IgG; IgM does not cross.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgG does cross the placenta and gives passive immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IDO breaks down tryptophan, not antibodies.

questions.stem: A mother asks why her healthy newborn is relatively protected from infections for the first several months of life. The passive immunity comes from maternal antibodies transferred across the placenta mainly during which period?

explanation.summary: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta mainly in the last trimester, giving passive immunity for several months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the fetal immune system is not fully developed, maternal IgG passes through the placenta during the last trimester, providing passive immunity that lasts several months after delivery while the infant's immune system matures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Days 8-9 are the time of implantation, before a functioning placenta exists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The first 10 weeks are the corpus luteum-dependent phase; IgG transfer occurs mainly later.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Placental transfer occurs before delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lecture places IgG transfer in the last trimester.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes for her first prenatal visit. The first day of her last menstrual period was exactly 10 weeks ago. She has regular 28-day cycles, and she believes conception occurred about 2 weeks after that date. Which gestational age should be documented in her chart?

explanation.summary: Gestational age is counted in completed weeks from the first day of the LMP, not from conception.
explanation.whyCorrect: By convention, gestational age is expressed in completed weeks from the first day of the last menstrual period. Because ovulation and conception occur about 2 weeks after the LMP, the fertilization age is roughly 2 weeks less than the gestational age; this is why the estimated delivery date at 40 weeks corresponds to about 38 weeks of in utero life.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 8 weeks is the approximate fertilization (conception) age, not the conventionally documented gestational age.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 9 weeks has no basis; gestational age is dated from the first day of the LMP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 11 weeks overestimates; exactly 10 weeks have passed since the first day of the LMP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 12 weeks would add 2 weeks rather than dating from the LMP itself.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman learns she is pregnant after taking a medication with known teratogenic potential throughout the past month. Her gestational age is 6 weeks. Exposure at this point in pregnancy carries the greatest risk of congenital anomalies chiefly because it coincides with which process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attainment of fetal viability outside the uterus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Development of most embryonic organ systems

choices.label: C
choices.text: Final maturation of the fetal lungs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quickening and rapid gain in fetal weight

explanation.summary: Toxic exposures in the first trimester (embryonic period) are most likely to cause congenital abnormalities because most organ systems form then.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first trimester includes the embryonic period (fertilization weeks 3-8), during which most of the organ systems develop. Therefore toxic exposures at this time are the most likely to produce congenital abnormalities; the fetal period begins in week 9 and continues to delivery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viability is reached at 22-24 weeks, well after this exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fetal lung maturity is not typically complete until about 36 weeks, in the third trimester.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The placenta takes over progesterone production at about 10 weeks; this is not what makes early exposures teratogenic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Quickening is first perceived at about 20 weeks, in the second trimester.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman plans to conceive in the next few months. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defects and takes no chronic medications. Which folic acid regimen is recommended for her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 400 μg daily, from at least 1 month preconception to end of first trimester

choices.label: B
choices.text: 400 μg daily, starting at the 18-20 week fetal anatomy ultrasound examination

choices.label: C
choices.text: 400 μg daily, starting once pregnancy is confirmed and continuing to delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Higher-dose daily, from 3 months preconception and continuing through delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: None needed, provided a prenatal vitamin is begun at 12 weeks of gestation

explanation.summary: Average-risk patients should take 400 μg folic acid daily from at least 1 month before conception through the end of the first trimester.
explanation.whyCorrect: The neural tube closes about 28 days after conception, often before a patient realizes she is pregnant. To lower NTD risk, those planning pregnancy are advised to take 400 μg of folic acid daily beginning at least 1 month before conception and continuing until the end of the first trimester. Higher doses for longer durations are reserved for high-risk patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: By 18-20 weeks neural tube closure is long complete, so starting then gives no NTD protection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Starting at confirmation of pregnancy is too late; the neural tube may already have closed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Higher-dose, longer regimens are for high-risk patients (prior NTD, anti-seizure drugs, strong family history), which she is not.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting until 12 weeks misses the preconception and early-embryonic window when folate prevents NTDs.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman at 17 weeks' gestation undergoes a quad screen. Results show decreased alpha-fetoprotein, decreased estriol, increased hCG, and increased inhibin A. This pattern is most consistent with which fetal condition?

explanation.summary: Quad screen in trisomy 21: low AFP, low estriol, high hCG, high inhibin A.
explanation.whyCorrect: The quad screen (15-22 weeks) measures AFP, hCG, estriol and inhibin A in maternal serum to estimate aneuploidy risk. Trisomy 21 classically shows decreased AFP and estriol with increased hCG and inhibin A.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anencephaly is an open neural tube defect, which elevates rather than lowers AFP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cystic fibrosis is evaluated by carrier screening of the parents, not by quad screen markers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Open neural tube defects raise AFP; this patient's AFP is decreased.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trisomy 18 shows decreases in all markers, including hCG, rather than elevated hCG and inhibin A.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has a cell-free DNA test reported as high risk for trisomy 21. She wants a definitive answer as early in pregnancy as possible. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat cell-free DNA testing in 4 weeks

explanation.summary: A positive cfDNA screen requires diagnostic confirmation; at 10-13 weeks the diagnostic option is CVS.
explanation.whyCorrect: cfDNA is a screening test; a high-risk result requires confirmation with diagnostic (or postnatal) testing. Chorionic villus sampling is performed at 10-13 weeks and uses an ultrasound-guided needle to obtain placental tissue for direct genetic analysis, so it gives the earliest definitive answer at 12 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amniocentesis is diagnostic but is performed at 15-22 weeks, not at 12 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carrier screening detects parental single-gene carrier status (eg, CF, SMA), not fetal aneuploidy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The quad screen is another screening test and is now largely replaced by cfDNA; it cannot confirm aneuploidy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeating a screening test does not provide a diagnosis; a positive screen should prompt diagnostic testing.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation by an early dating ultrasound is seen for a routine visit. The pregnancy is progressing normally. On abdominal examination, where is the uterine fundus expected to be palpated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the level of the maternal umbilicus

choices.label: B
choices.text: At the level of the xiphoid process

choices.label: D
choices.text: Midway between the umbilicus and xiphoid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Still contained within the bony pelvis

explanation.summary: At 20 weeks the fundus reaches the umbilicus, and fundal height (cm) approximately equals gestational weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the second trimester the uterus expands into the abdomen, and at 20 weeks the fundus is at the level of the maternal umbilicus. Fundal height, measured from the symphysis pubis to the fundus, should be about 20 cm at 20 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A fundus at the xiphoid would indicate a far more advanced pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The uterus becomes just palpable above the pubic symphysis at about 12 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A fundus above the umbilicus would be expected later than 20 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The uterus stays within the bony pelvis only in the first trimester.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation has a venous glucose level measured 1 hour after drinking a 50-gram glucose solution. The result is elevated. She has no polyuria or polydipsia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diagnose GDM and start dietary therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obtain a fasting urine glucose level

explanation.summary: An elevated 1-hour 50-g screen is followed by a 100-g 3-hour GTT; GDM is diagnosed only if that is also elevated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Between 24 and 28 weeks, patients are screened for GDM with a 1-hour venous glucose after a 50-g oral load. If elevated, a 100-g 3-hour glucose tolerance test follows, and an elevated result on that test meets criteria for GDM.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Treatment is premature; the screening result has not yet been confirmed by the diagnostic 3-hour test.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An elevated 1-hour screen alone does not meet criteria for GDM.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urine glucose is not part of the described two-step GDM testing sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Delaying to repeat the screen postpones diagnosis; the next step is the 100-g 3-hour test.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman, G2P1, is seen at 28 weeks' gestation. Her blood type is O, RhD-negative. An indirect Coombs test in the first trimester was negative, and a repeat indirect Coombs test today is again negative for anti-D antibodies. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amniocentesis to determine fetal RhD status

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct Coombs test on maternal red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serial ultrasound surveillance for fetal anemia

explanation.summary: RhD-negative patients with a negative antibody screen receive RhoGAM at 28 weeks to prevent anti-D formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: RhD-negative patients have an indirect Coombs test in the first trimester and again in the late second trimester. If the antibody screen remains negative, RhoGAM is given at 28 weeks to block the patient from forming anti-D antibodies, protecting future pregnancies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Invasive fetal testing is not part of routine management of an unsensitized RhD-negative patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The indirect Coombs test detects circulating maternal antibodies; a direct Coombs on maternal cells adds nothing here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Withholding prophylaxis leaves her at risk of sensitization; RhoGAM is indicated at 28 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serial ultrasound for fetal anemia is indicated when anti-D antibodies are present at elevated titers, not when the screen is negative.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 36 weeks' gestation has a rectovaginal swab that grows Streptococcus agalactiae. She has no symptoms and no drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No treatment, as colonization is harmless

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oral amoxicillin now, then repeat the swab

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treat her partner and rescreen at 38 weeks

explanation.summary: GBS-positive patients receive intrapartum antibiotics (penicillin), cutting neonatal infection by about 80%.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACOG recommends universal GBS screening at 36 to 37 6/7 weeks by rectovaginal swab. Patients who screen positive are treated during labor with antibiotics (penicillin unless allergy requires an alternative), which reduces neonatal infection by approximately 80%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although colonization is harmless to her, GBS can cause neonatal septicemia and pneumonia, so intrapartum treatment is indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Treating before labor is not recommended because colonization is transient and likely to recur before delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cesarean delivery is not the described strategy; intrapartum antibiotics are.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Partner treatment and rescreening are not part of the recommended approach.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman is diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus at 27 weeks' gestation. Her glucose control over the next several weeks is poor. Her first-trimester course was uncomplicated. Which of the following is her newborn most at risk of developing?

explanation.summary: GDM causes fetal hyperinsulinemia and neonatal hypoglycemia, but not major malformations, because hyperglycemia begins after organogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta, and the fetus responds with hyperinsulinemia. GDM therefore raises the risk of macrosomia, fetal hyperinsulinemia with neonatal hypoglycemia, and neonatal respiratory distress. Unlike pregestational diabetes, GDM is not typically associated with major congenital malformations because the hyperglycemia occurs after organogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neural tube defects arise from failed closure about 28 days after conception, long before GDM develops.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Major congenital malformations are associated with pregestational diabetes, not GDM arising after organogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fetal hemolytic anemia results from maternal anti-D antibodies, not maternal hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neonatal pertussis risk relates to lack of passive immunity (addressed by maternal Tdap), not GDM.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman at 8 weeks' gestation reports daily nausea and occasional vomiting, worst in the mornings. She asks which hormone is responsible. Rising levels of which hormone correlate with these symptoms?

explanation.summary: High beta-hCG levels from the placenta correlate with nausea and vomiting of early pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: beta-hCG is a glycoprotein hormone released by the placenta a few days after implantation. Its high levels in early pregnancy are likely directly or indirectly responsible for nausea and vomiting, which typically recede in the second trimester as beta-hCG levels off.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AFP is produced by the fetal liver and is used to screen for NTDs and aneuploidy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Estriol is a quad screen marker, not the hormone linked to early-pregnancy nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibin A is a quad screen marker, not the hormone linked to early-pregnancy nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progesterone supports the endometrium (taken over by the placenta at about 10 weeks) but is not the hormone correlated with morning sickness.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation received a low-risk cell-free DNA result for common aneuploidies. Her cousin was born with spina bifida, and she asks whether this result means her fetus does not have a neural tube defect. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It does not evaluate NTD risk; maternal serum screening can

choices.label: B
choices.text: It estimates NTD risk only when combined with carrier screening

choices.label: C
choices.text: It must be confirmed with CVS before NTDs can be excluded

choices.label: D
choices.text: It rules out open NTDs with high sensitivity and specificity

choices.label: E
choices.text: NTDs can be evaluated only by examination after delivery

explanation.summary: cfDNA screens for common aneuploidies but does not assess NTD risk; serum screening (AFP) +/- NT estimates NTD risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-invasive prenatal testing with cfDNA sequences placental DNA fragments in maternal blood to detect common aneuploidies, but it does not assess neural tube defect risk. Maternal serum screening (with or without nuchal translucency) provides a risk estimate for both aneuploidy and NTDs, and elevated AFP is the marker of open NTDs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carrier screening assesses parental carrier status for conditions such as CF and SMA, not NTD risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CVS is used to confirm a positive aneuploidy screen; a low-risk cfDNA result does not require CVS, and CVS is not the NTD assessment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: cfDNA has high sensitivity and specificity for common aneuploidies, not for neural tube defects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NTDs can be assessed prenatally, for example by serum AFP screening or amniotic fluid AFP.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 40 weeks' gestation is admitted in active labor. This is her first pregnancy, and she has never given birth. Which set of terms best describes her?

explanation.summary: First pregnancy = primigravid; no prior live birth = nulliparous; in labor = parturient (G1P0).
explanation.whyCorrect: Primigravid means pregnant for the first time, nulliparous means never having given birth to a live child, and parturient refers to a patient in labor. In GTPAL shorthand she is G1P0.

whyWrongByChoice.A: She is neither multigravid nor parous; she has had no prior births.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Multigravid means pregnant more than once; this is her first pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nulligravid means never pregnant, which contradicts her current pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although primigravid, she has had no prior births and is therefore nulliparous.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is 9 weeks pregnant. She has had two previous pregnancies, both ending in spontaneous loss at 8 weeks, and she has never given birth. She is not in labor. Which description of her obstetric status is correct?

explanation.summary: More than one pregnancy = multigravid; no live birth = nulliparous, regardless of prior losses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Multigravid means having been pregnant more than once, which applies to her third pregnancy. Nulliparous means never having given birth to a live child; her early losses do not count as births.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Parturient refers to a patient in labor, which she is not.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nulligravid means never pregnant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primigravid means pregnant for the first time; this is her third pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: She is neither primigravid nor in labor.

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old woman at 37 weeks' gestation with an uncomplicated pregnancy asks to schedule an elective delivery next week for convenience. Compared with a birth at 39 weeks, an infant delivered at 38 weeks is at higher risk for which of the following?

explanation.summary: Full term begins at 39 weeks; earlier births carry more respiratory and feeding problems and infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACOG and SMFM now consider a pregnancy full term at 39 weeks. Babies born before this point are at higher risk for respiratory and feeding problems and are more susceptible to infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Structural malformations arise during organogenesis, not from delivery timing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrosomia is associated with post-term pregnancy and GDM, not early delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Declining placental function with meconium aspiration is a post-term (42 weeks or later) risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NTDs arise about 28 days after conception and are unaffected by delivery timing.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman, G1P0, is at 42 weeks 1 day of gestation and has not gone into labor. Which underlying process best explains her fetus's increased risk of distress and meconium aspiration?

explanation.summary: Post-term (42 weeks or later) pregnancy risks stem from gradually declining placental oxygen and nutrient delivery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Post-term infants are delivered at 42 weeks or later. Prolonged pregnancy increases fetal and neonatal risk because placental function may gradually decline, reducing oxygen and nutrient delivery, which raises the risk of fetal distress, meconium aspiration, macrosomia and other adverse outcomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fetal hyperinsulinemia is a consequence of GDM, not of prolonged gestation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-D antibodies cause fetal hemolytic anemia in sensitized RhD-negative patients.
whyWrongByChoice.D: beta-hCG levels off after the first trimester and is not the mechanism of post-term risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GBS colonization risks neonatal sepsis and pneumonia, not the placental insufficiency of post-term pregnancy.

questions.stem: Early in pregnancy, progesterone must be maintained to prevent shedding of the endometrium. At approximately what gestational age does the placenta take over progesterone production?

explanation.summary: The placenta forms and takes over progesterone production at about 10 weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: At about 10 weeks, the placenta forms and takes over progesterone production to support the developing fetus and prevent shedding of the endometrium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: At 4 weeks the placenta has not yet assumed progesterone production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 20 weeks is the time of quickening and fundus at the umbilicus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 28 weeks marks the start of the third trimester and RhoGAM administration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 36 weeks is when fetal lung maturity and GBS screening occur.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida at 16 weeks' gestation is worried because she has not yet felt the baby move. Her ultrasound today is normal. At approximately what gestational age do patients first become aware of fetal movement?

explanation.summary: Quickening, the first maternal perception of fetal movement, occurs at about 20 weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: At approximately 20 weeks, patients first become aware of fetal movement, called quickening. Not feeling movement at 16 weeks is therefore expected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: At 8 weeks fetal movement is not perceived by the mother.
whyWrongByChoice.B: At 12 weeks the uterus is only just palpable above the pubic symphysis; movement is not yet felt.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 28 weeks is later than the typical onset of quickening.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 36 weeks is far later than the typical onset of quickening.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation has a repeat complete blood count showing a hemoglobin level below the normal range. She takes a prenatal vitamin inconsistently. Which of the following best explains why this finding is common in pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic blood loss from hemorrhoids and varicosities

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expanded maternal blood volume and fetal iron demand

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folic acid supplements displacing iron from absorption

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal anti-D antibodies destroying maternal red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy persisting to week 26

explanation.summary: Iron-deficiency anemia is screened for in pregnancy because of blood-volume expansion and the fetus's large iron requirement.
explanation.whyCorrect: Screening for iron-deficiency anemia is done in the second trimester because it is common, given expansion of the maternal blood volume and the significant amount of iron needed for fetal development. A repeat CBC guides adequate iron supplementation or further work-up.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemorrhoids and varicosities reflect venous congestion from uterine compression, not the usual cause of pregnancy anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folic acid is recommended to prevent NTDs; it is not described as impairing iron absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-D antibodies target fetal RhD-positive red cells, causing fetal, not maternal, hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nausea and vomiting typically recede in the second trimester as beta-hCG levels off.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman asks why she was told to begin folic acid before trying to conceive rather than waiting until her first prenatal visit at 8-10 weeks. Which fact best supports the preconception recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal liver AFP production requires stored folate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate crosses the placenta only before implantation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate is required for placental progesterone synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Folate stores later prevent gestational diabetes

choices.label: E
choices.text: The neural tube closes about 28 days after conception

explanation.summary: The neural tube closes ~28 days after conception, often before a pregnancy is recognized, so folate must already be on board.
explanation.whyCorrect: The fetal neural tube closes approximately 28 days after conception, shortly after the first missed period, when a patient may not realize she is pregnant. Incomplete closure causes anencephaly or spina bifida, so folic acid is begun at least 1 month before conception.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AFP is a marker used to detect NTDs, not a reason to start folate early.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate transfer is not restricted to the pre-implantation period; timing matters because of neural tube closure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Placental progesterone production begins at about 10 weeks and is not the rationale for folate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folic acid is recommended to prevent neural tube defects, not GDM.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy controlled on an anti-seizure medication is planning a pregnancy. Which folic acid recommendation is most appropriate for her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 400 μg daily only during the embryonic period

choices.label: B
choices.text: 400 μg daily, beginning at 12 weeks of gestation

choices.label: C
choices.text: A higher dose for a longer duration than standard

choices.label: D
choices.text: No folic acid until her regimen is reviewed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standard 400 μg daily, as for average-risk patients

explanation.summary: Patients at high risk for NTDs (eg, on anti-seizure medications) need a higher folic acid dose for a longer duration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Those at high risk for NTDs, including patients with a prior affected pregnancy, a strong family history, or certain medications such as anti-seizure drugs, are advised to take a higher dose of folic acid for a longer duration than the standard 400 μg regimen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 400 μg limited to the embryonic period is both too low and too short for a high-risk patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Starting at 12 weeks is after neural tube closure and too late for any patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Withholding folic acid leaves a high-risk patient unprotected against NTDs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The standard dose is for average-risk patients; anti-seizure medication places her at high risk.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has routine studies at her first prenatal visit. A urine culture grows significant numbers of Escherichia coli. She has no dysuria, frequency, fever, or flank pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No treatment, because she is asymptomatic

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obtain a renal ultrasound before deciding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat the urine culture with the 36-week swab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Treat only if fever or flank pain develops

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy should be treated to prevent pyelonephritis, preterm birth and low birth weight.
explanation.whyCorrect: All pregnant patients are screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria with an early urine culture; most cases are due to E coli. Untreated, it increases the risk of acute pyelonephritis, preterm birth and low-birth-weight infants, so significant bacteriuria is treated with appropriate antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absence of symptoms does not remove the risk; asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Imaging is not required before treating screen-detected bacteriuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delaying until 36 weeks exposes her to pyelonephritis and preterm birth; the 36-week swab screens for GBS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Waiting for pyelonephritis to develop defeats the purpose of screening.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman who tracks her ovulation believes fertilization occurred 9 days ago. She wants the earliest possible confirmation of pregnancy. Which statement about hCG detection is most accurate at this time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: hCG appears only once the placenta forms at 10 weeks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neither serum nor urine hCG is detectable until 4 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum and urine hCG both first appear at about 20 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum hCG may be detectable now; urine at 12-14 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urine hCG is detectable now, but serum not for a week

explanation.summary: hCG appears in maternal blood 8-10 days after fertilization and in urine about 12-14 days after fertilization.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy testing detects hCG in maternal body fluids. hCG can be detected in maternal blood as early as 8-10 days after fertilization and begins to appear in urine approximately 12-14 days after fertilization, which is when at-home urine tests become positive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: hCG is released a few days after implantation, long before the placenta takes over progesterone at 10 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum hCG can be detected as early as 8-10 days after fertilization, well before 4 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both serum (8-10 days) and urine (12-14 days) hCG appear earlier than 20 days.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The order is reversed: blood detection precedes urine detection.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with previously regular menstrual cycles reports that she has not had a period in 3 months. She is otherwise well. Which of the following is the most appropriate first diagnostic step?

explanation.summary: Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea, so an hCG test comes first.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary amenorrhea is the absence of menses in a person who previously had menstrual cycles. Because pregnancy is its most common cause, pregnancy testing is the first diagnostic step in any reproductive-age patient with missed periods.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Imaging is not the first step; pregnancy must be excluded first with an hCG test.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A progestin challenge is not the initial step before a pregnancy test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gonadotropin testing is not the first step before excluding pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolactin testing is not the first step before excluding pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 8 weeks' gestation is identified at her first visit as being at increased risk for preeclampsia. She is counseled to take low-dose aspirin. At what gestational age should aspirin be started?

explanation.summary: Low-dose aspirin for increased preeclampsia risk is started at 12 weeks and continued to 36 weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients at increased risk for preeclampsia are advised to initiate low-dose aspirin at 12 weeks of gestation, continuing through 36 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 24-28 weeks is the window for GDM screening, not aspirin initiation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 28 weeks is when RhoGAM is given to unsensitized RhD-negative patients.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 36 weeks is when low-dose aspirin is stopped, not started.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aspirin is not started at 8 weeks; initiation is at 12 weeks.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation undergoes the carrier screening recommended for all pregnant patients. She is found to carry a single pathogenic allele associated with cystic fibrosis. Her family history is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell-free DNA to confirm her carrier status

choices.label: D
choices.text: Offer carrier screening to her partner

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat her own screen on an expanded panel

explanation.summary: Carrier screening is sequential: screen the pregnant patient first, then test the partner if she is positive.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACOG recommends carrier screening of all pregnant patients for cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy and hemoglobinopathies regardless of ethnicity. Screening is typically sequential: the pregnant individual is tested first, and the partner is tested if she is positive, since the fetus is at risk only if both are carriers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amniocentesis is premature before knowing whether the partner is also a carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.B: cfDNA screens for fetal aneuploidy; it does not confirm parental carrier status.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Invasive fetal testing is premature before knowing whether the partner is also a carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeating her own screen adds little; the partner's status determines fetal risk.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation has a quad screen showing decreased alpha-fetoprotein, decreased hCG, decreased estriol, and decreased inhibin A. Which fetal condition is this pattern most consistent with?

explanation.summary: Quad screen in trisomy 18: all markers decreased (AFP, hCG, estriol, +/- inhibin A).
explanation.whyCorrect: In the quad screen, trisomy 18 shows decreases in all markers: AFP, hCG and estriol, with or without decreased inhibin A. This contrasts with trisomy 21, where hCG and inhibin A are increased.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Open NTDs are characterized by increased AFP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: RhD alloimmunization is detected by the indirect Coombs test, not quad screen markers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SMA is assessed by parental carrier screening, not maternal serum markers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trisomy 21 shows increased hCG and inhibin A, not decreases.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 17 weeks' gestation undergoes amniocentesis because of concern for an open neural tube defect. The amniotic fluid concentration of alpha-fetoprotein is elevated. This protein is produced chiefly by which fetal organ?

explanation.summary: AFP is produced by the fetal liver; elevated amniotic fluid AFP diagnoses an open NTD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amniocentesis, performed at 15-22 weeks, can diagnose neural tube defects by detecting an increase in alpha-fetoprotein, which is produced by the fetal liver, in the amniotic fluid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The fetal adrenal gland is not the source of AFP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The fetal kidney is not the source of AFP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The fetal lung is not the source of AFP; lung maturity is reached by about 36 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The placenta produces beta-hCG and, from about 10 weeks, progesterone, not AFP.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 21 weeks' gestation asks from what point her baby could be expected to survive outside the womb if born early, given modern obstetric and neonatal care. Which range is most accurate?

explanation.summary: Viability, the youngest gestational age at which survival outside the womb is expected, is now 22-24 weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viability is defined as the youngest gestational age at which survival outside the womb could be expected. With modern obstetric and neonatal care, this is now between 22 and 24 weeks, within the second trimester.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 16-18 weeks is before viability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 18-20 weeks is the time of the anatomy ultrasound and quickening, still before viability.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 28-30 weeks is well after the threshold of viability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 34-36 weeks approaches fetal lung maturity, not the threshold of viability.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation, dated by a first-trimester crown-rump length, has a fundal height of 24 cm. Her blood pressure is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reassurance; this is within the expected range

choices.label: C
choices.text: Redate the pregnancy to 24 weeks' gestation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ultrasound to assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid

explanation.summary: Fundal height in cm should approximate gestational weeks; a discrepancy prompts ultrasound for fetal growth or fluid disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fundal height, measured from the symphysis pubis to the fundus, assesses fetal size and amniotic fluid volume, and in centimeters should approximate gestational age in weeks. A measurement that differs from expected (24 cm at 30 weeks) warrants ultrasound to assess for disorders of fetal growth or amniotic fluid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Invasive genetic testing is not the initial evaluation of a size-dates discrepancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 6-cm lag is not within the expected correlation of centimeters to weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Early ultrasound dating is reliable; the discrepancy suggests a growth or fluid problem, not wrong dates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucose screening does not evaluate the cause of a small fundal height.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with a pre-pregnancy BMI of 22 kg/m2 is pregnant with a single fetus. She asks how much weight she should gain over the entire pregnancy. What is the recommended total weight gain?

explanation.summary: With a normal pre-pregnancy BMI (18.5-24.9), recommended total gain for a singleton is 25-35 lb.
explanation.whyCorrect: For a singleton pregnancy in a patient with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI of 18.5-24.9, the recommended total weight gain is 25-35 pounds. Weight is tracked at regular visits to identify patients who need counseling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 11-20 lb is below the recommendation for a normal-BMI singleton pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 15-25 lb is below the recommendation for a normal-BMI singleton pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 20-25 lb is below the recommended range for normal BMI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 35-45 lb exceeds the recommendation for a normal-BMI singleton pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman, G3P2, at 24 weeks' gestation is RhD-negative. Her indirect Coombs test shows anti-D antibodies at an elevated titer. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Give RhoGAM now to neutralize the antibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immediate delivery to prevent fetal hemolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reassure her that antibodies do not cross the placenta

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat the antibody screen at 28 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serial ultrasound monitoring for fetal anemia

explanation.summary: Elevated anti-D titers require serial ultrasound monitoring for fetal anemia; RhoGAM is for unsensitized patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-D antibodies from prior exposure to RhD-positive fetal blood can cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells, causing fetal hemolytic anemia. When anti-D antibodies are present at elevated titers, serial ultrasound monitoring to assess for fetal anemia is required.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RhoGAM prevents antibody formation in unsensitized patients; it does not help once she is already sensitized.
whyWrongByChoice.B: At 24 weeks, surveillance for fetal anemia, not immediate delivery, is the described management.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-D antibodies do cross the placenta, which is why they cause fetal hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Simply rescreening delays needed fetal surveillance in a sensitized patient.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation asks why she should receive the Tdap vaccine now, when her newborn could simply be vaccinated after birth. Which explanation is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Maternal IgA crosses the placenta and coats the fetal airway mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and passively protects the newborn

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal IgM crosses the placenta and passively protects the newborn

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vaccine clears maternal colonization before labor and delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaccine antigen crosses the placenta and actively immunizes the fetus

explanation.summary: Maternal Tdap at 27-36 weeks gives the newborn passive IgG protection against pertussis before the infant can be vaccinated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tdap is given at 27-36 weeks, ideally early in that window. Maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and provide passive immune protection to the fetus and newborn against pertussis (whooping cough) before the infant can receive the vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The antibodies described as crossing the placenta are IgG, not IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The protective antibodies that cross the placenta are IgG, not IgM.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clearing maternal colonization before labor describes GBS management, not Tdap.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protection is passive via maternal antibody, not active fetal immunization.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation reports painful hemorrhoids and newly visible varicose veins in both legs. Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated. Which of the following is the primary cause of these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Declining placental function raising venous tone

explanation.summary: Third-trimester reflux, edema, hemorrhoids and varicosities result from extrinsic compression by the enlarged uterus.
